screens.title: Smart Contracts and Solidity — An Introduction
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts are small programs that run on the blockchain and enforce rules without intermediaries. In practice that means once a contract is deployed it will execute exactly as coded, for anyone who calls it, on every node — a property that delivers trust but also requires discipline. In this lesson we focus on the Solidity basics you need to write, compile, and deploy simple contracts safely. You will learn the building blocks of a contract: the pragma compiler line, the contract block itself, state variables that persist on-chain, functions that change or read state, and events that let off-chain applications react without repeatedly polling state. You will also see the typical artifacts produced by compilation — the ABI and the bytecode — and why they matter to front‑end code like Web3. js. As we proceed, keep two ideas in mind: immutability means code can’t be changed after deployment, and deterministic execution means the same inputs produce the same outputs across all nodes. By the end you should be able to write a minimal contract, compile it in Remix, and explain the implications of publishing code on-chain. What would you do differently when every change is permanent?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Introduction
Smart Contracts and Solidity — An Introduction
Understand the guarantees and responsibilities of writing code that lives on-chain.
In this lesson

You will learn what a smart contract is, key Solidity constructs, how compilation produces ABI and bytecode, and the deployment implications of immutability. Practical Remix steps will show the full authoring loop.

Why this matters
Smart contracts replace trusted intermediaries. That shifts responsibility to code quality, testing, and careful design.
Explore Key Topics
Immutability
Code cannot be changed after deployment; bugs require new deployments.
Solidity Basics
Pragma, contract blocks, state variables, functions, and events form the core structure.
Events & ABI
Events emit logs for off‑chain listeners; the ABI defines how to call contract functions.
Visual Concept
On-chain code
Bytecode stored at a contract address
State
Persistent variables live in contract storage and can be changed by functions.
Events
Emit logs to notify off‑chain systems without heavy querying.
Coming up
We’ll move from definitions to hands-on code examples in Remix, inspecting ABI and bytecode and understanding errors to avoid before deployment.

screens.title: What is a Smart Contract?
screens.narratorSegment: A smart contract is a program that lives on a blockchain and executes automatically according to its code. It is self‑executing in the sense that the rules and outcomes are written into the code itself; once deployed, that code runs deterministically across every node. The chapter emphasizes three important guarantees: immutability, transparency, and deterministic execution. Immutability means the deployed code cannot be changed, so any logic you publish becomes permanent. Transparency means transactions and state changes are publicly verifiable on the blockchain, enabling anyone to audit behavior. Deterministic execution ensures the same inputs produce the same results across all nodes, which is how trustless agreement is achieved. A helpful analogy is a vending machine: drop in the right coin and the machine dispenses the selected item exactly as programmed. A common misconception is to confuse immutability of code with immutability of state; while the code cannot be changed, the contract’s state can be updated through function calls governed by its logic. Finally, consider why these guarantees matter: they remove intermediaries but place the burden of correctness on code quality, testing, and audit. Reflect: what checks would you add before making a contract public?

keyIdea.text: A smart contract is a self‑executing, immutable program stored on the blockchain that enforces rules transparently and deterministically.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is a Smart Contract?
Definition
Smart Contract
A program stored on the blockchain that executes rules automatically and deterministically.
Immutability
Code cannot be changed after deployment; choose and test carefully before publishing.
Deterministic Execution
Given the same inputs, the contract yields the same outputs on every node.
Transparency
Transactions and state changes are publicly verifiable and auditable.
Analogy & Example
Analogy: A vending machine is a simple way to think about a smart contract. You provide the correct input, the machine executes a fixed set of rules, and you receive the result without intermediaries.
Common misconception
People sometimes think immutability prevents all changes. In fact, immutability applies to the program code; the contract’s state can still change through transactions that call its functions if the contract allows it.
Key Takeaway

Smart contracts replace intermediaries with code, so correctness and testing are essential before deployment.

screens.title: How Solidity Becomes On-Chain Code
screens.narratorSegment: When you author Solidity you start with a pragma line that pins the compiler version, then write a contract block containing state, functions, and events. The compiler translates that human-readable Solidity into EVM bytecode and produces an ABI that describes the contract’s functions and events in a machine-readable JSON array. Deploying the compiled bytecode publishes it to the blockchain as a contract account with a unique address; that address is what your front-end libraries call. The ABI is essential for Web3. js because it tells the library how to encode function calls and decode event logs. In practice, use Remix or another compiler to generate the artifacts. Inspect the compilation details to copy the ABI and the bytecode. A common misconception is to confuse the ABI with bytecode — the ABI is an interface description, the bytecode is the executable that runs on the EVM. Finally, remember deployment permanence: once the bytecode is stored at an address, the code itself cannot be changed. If you discover a bug later, the remedy is to deploy a corrected contract and migrate state if needed. How would you design an upgrade path knowing code is immutable?

keyIdea.title: Compilation pipeline
keyIdea.text: Solidity → Compiler → ABI + Bytecode → Deploy → Contract Account (immutable bytecode at an address).

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Compilation & Deployment
Step-by-step
1. Author (pragma & contract)
Write Solidity with a pragma version to ensure compiler compatibility.
2. Compile (ABI + Bytecode)
Compiler emits ABI and bytecode. ABI is for callers; bytecode is the executable on the EVM.
3. Deploy (contract account)
Publishing bytecode creates a contract account with a unique address that holds the immutable code.
Concrete example
In Remix, compile a contract and open Compilation Details. Copy the ABI JSON to use in Web3.js. Copy bytecode if you need to deploy programmatically. If you later find a bug in the bytecode at that address, you must deploy a new contract with corrected code.
Key Takeaway

ABI describes the interface; bytecode is the executable. Deployment makes code permanent.

screens.title: Solidity Contract Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A Solidity source file is organized much like a small class-based program. It usually starts with a pragma declaration that sets the compiler version. Next comes the contract block — the primary container that holds state variables, functions, and events. State variables are stored on-chain; declaring a variable as public makes a simple getter available automatically. Functions encapsulate logic and can be marked with visibility and mutability keywords such as public, private, view, pure, or payable. Events are declared to emit log entries for off‑chain listeners. A helpful mental hierarchy is: file → contract → state + functions + events. For example, a state variable like uint public storedData is permanently stored on-chain and can be updated by a function like set. Events do not change state but provide an efficient mechanism for external applications to react to changes without repeatedly querying stored values. A common mistake is to mix up mutability keywords: marking a function view does not allow it to change state. When designing contracts, map the responsibilities of each element clearly so off‑chain code and users will interact with your contract safely and predictably.

keyIdea.text: Solidity files contain a pragma, contract block, state variables persist on-chain, functions define behavior, and events provide off‑chain notifications.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Contract Structure
Hierarchy
Pragma
Pins compiler version, ensuring compatibility with language features.
Contract block
Holds persistent state, functions for behavior, and event declarations.
State variable
Stored in contract storage and persists across transactions.
Function
Executable logic that may read or modify state, and may be payable to accept Ether.
Event
Logs an occurrence for off‑chain listeners to react to changes efficiently.
Example Scenario
Imagine a storedData variable and two functions: one sets a new value, the other returns the value. Marking the getter as view indicates it will not change state, making it free to call off‑chain. Marking a setter as payable would allow it to receive Ether if the contract is designed to accept funds.
Common mistake

Confusing view and payable: view cannot modify state; payable allows Ether transfers but does not imply state changes on its own.

screens.title: SimpleStorage: Read, Write, and Emit
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a minimal contract to ground the structure in real code. The contract declares a public unsigned integer state variable, functions to set and get its value, an event declaration, and a function that updates the variable while emitting that event. The public state variable produces a getter automatically, so off‑chain code can read storage without writing a custom function. The setter function updates state and will cost gas when called on-chain. The update-and-emit function captures the old value, stores the new one, and emits an event that logs the change and the changer address. Events are efficient for notifying front‑end code because a dApp can subscribe to event logs rather than continuously reading state. A common misconception is assuming events themselves change contract state — they do not; they are logs. Finally, before deploying any contract with state-changing functions think about who should be allowed to call them and under what conditions. This walkthrough connects the code to the real operational and integration concerns you will face while building dApps. keyIdea.title: Practical code idea
keyIdea.text: A simple contract demonstrates state variables, setters/getters, and events used to notify off‑chain systems when state changes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › SimpleStorage Walkthrough
Code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
  uint public storedData; // State variable, publicly readable

  function set(uint x) public {
    storedData = x;
  }

  function get() public view returns (uint) {
    return storedData;
  }

  event DataChanged(uint indexed oldValue, uint newValue, address changer);

  function updateDataAndEmit(uint _newValue) public {
    uint _oldValue = storedData;
    storedData = _newValue;
    emit DataChanged(_oldValue, _newValue, msg.sender);
  }
}
Explainer bullets
  • storedData is a state variable persisted on-chain and exposed via an automatic getter because it is public.
  • set modifies state and requires a transaction with gas when called on-chain.
  • get is a view function and does not change state; it can be called off‑chain without a transaction.
  • event records a log that off‑chain apps can subscribe to; emitting does not change contract storage directly.
Key Takeaway

Use events to notify off‑chain systems and respect view/payable differences when designing functions that read or change state.

Common mistake

Believe that emitting an event is a substitute for storing important state. Events are logs and can be pruned by clients; critical data should live in contract storage when needed on-chain.

screens.title: MyFirstContract: Strings, Memory, and Events
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter offers a hands-on activity using a greeting contract to practice writing, compiling, and inspecting artifacts. In this contract a string state variable greeting holds text on-chain, a setter updates it using a memory parameter for safe temporary storage, and a getter returns the stored greeting as a view function. The contract also declares an event that logs the old and new greetings and the address that performed the update. When you compile this in Remix, pay attention to the compiler version matching your pragma and then open the compilation details to copy the ABI and bytecode. The ABI lists functions and events so front‑end code can encode function calls and decode logs. The bytecode is what will be published at the contract address when deployed. A frequent contrast to note: human‑readable Solidity vs machine‑readable bytecode — they represent the same logic but at different abstraction levels. When you complete this exercise, check that the ABI correctly lists the getter and the event, and that the contract responds as expected when calling set or change-and-log functions in the Remix deploy panel.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › MyFirstContract Exercise
Starter Code
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract MyFirstContract {
    string public greeting = "Hello, Cohortia!"; // A state variable

    function setGreeting(string memory _newGreeting) public {
        greeting = _newGreeting;
    }

    function getGreeting() public view returns (string memory) {
        return greeting;
    }

    event GreetingUpdated(string indexed oldGreeting, string newGreeting, address updater);

    function changeGreetingAndLog(string memory _newGreeting) public {
        string memory _oldGreeting = greeting;
        greeting = _newGreeting;
        emit GreetingUpdated(_oldGreeting, _newGreeting, msg.sender);
    }
}
What to inspect in Remix
  • Confirm the compiler version matches the pragma line before compiling.
  • Open Compilation Details and copy the ABI JSON for use with Web3.js.
  • Copy the bytecode if you plan to deploy programmatically or via scripts.
  • Use the deployed instance in Remix to call read functions for free and send transactions to update state.
Key Takeaway

The ABI connects your human-readable contract to front-end code; the bytecode is what you publish to create the immutable contract account.

screens.title: Common Solidity Data Types
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity provides a set of primitive and composite types you will use to model on‑chain data. The chapter lists the commonly used ones: unsigned and signed integers (uint, int), address, bool, string, bytes, mapping, struct, and enum. Use uint for counters or balances, and address to represent account identifiers. Booleans represent binary states, and strings or bytes hold textual or raw data when necessary. Mapping is a built-in key-value storage mechanism useful for lookups, while struct lets you bundle related fields into a single composite type. Enum defines a set of named constant values for limited states. A common design consideration is gas cost: larger or complex types cost more to store and update, so avoid storing large strings unless required. Another misconception is assuming mappings are iterable — they are not; mappings are optimized for lookup but do not provide built-in enumeration. Choose types with both correctness and on‑chain cost in mind. Think about how your front-end will read and present stored values, and how events might be used to emit human-friendly logs instead of expensive on‑chain storage in some cases.

keyIdea.title: Type guidance
keyIdea.text: Match Solidity types to the data model: use address for accounts, mapping for lookups, struct for records, and enum for constrained states; avoid unnecessary large storage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Data Types
Primitives
uint / int — integers for counters and numeric values.
address — 20-byte account identifier used for ownership and transfers.
bool — true/false flags for simple conditions.
string / bytes — text and raw data; use sparingly for gas reasons.
Composite Types
mapping — key-value store for fast lookups (not iterable).
struct — group related fields into a single type.
enum — define a limited set of state values for clarity.
Design notes
Large or complex data increases gas cost for storage and updates.
Mappings are not iterable — plan additional indexing via events if you need enumeration.
Choose types that map naturally to how off‑chain code reads and displays contract state.

screens.title: Function Visibility and Mutability
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding function visibility and mutability is crucial to controlling who can call your contract and what those calls may do. Visibility keywords determine who can invoke a function: public makes the function callable from everywhere, private restricts it to the contract that defines it, internal allows derived contracts to access it, and external optimizes for calls from other contracts or transactions. Mutability modifiers describe whether a function reads or changes state: view functions promise not to modify state and can be called off‑chain without a transaction; pure functions promise not to even read state and are purely computational. Payable marks a function as able to receive Ether; without it, any attempt to send Ether will revert. Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Visibility & Mutability
Visibility
public — accessible from anywhere, including external callers.
private — accessible only inside the contract that defines it.
internal — accessible inside the contract and derived contracts.
external — callable from external transactions and other contracts; optimized for calldata.
Mutability
view — reads state only; no state modification.
pure — does not read or modify state; deterministic computation only.
payable — allows the function to receive Ether; missing payable causes reversion if Ether is sent.
Common mistake
Marking a function public does not provide access control. Use explicit checks and modifiers to prevent unauthorized state changes.

screens.title: Events and Off‑Chain Communication
screens.narratorSegment: Events are a mechanism for contracts to record information that off‑chain applications can observe efficiently. When a contract emits an event, the data is stored in transaction logs that nodes keep; dApps and services listen for these logs rather than polling contract storage continuously. Events are especially useful for recording activity like state changes, transfers, or important actions where the front-end must react. In our examples the DataChanged or GreetingUpdated events log the previous value, the new value, and the address that made the change. Note that events do not change on‑chain storage — they are supplemental logs. A common misunderstanding is to use events as the primary source of truth for critical on‑chain data; events may be archived or indexed differently by clients, so store crucial data in contract state if the protocol requires on‑chain verification. Events are excellent for activity streams, UI updates, and efficient audit trails for off‑chain systems. When designing events, include indexed fields strategically so listeners can filter logs efficiently without scanning every block. Events and Off‑Chain Communication means use events to emit logs for off‑chain listeners; they do not modify contract state and are intended for efficient notification and indexing.. In practical terms, how contracts signal the outside world using logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Contract Deployment and Immutability
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a contract means publishing compiled bytecode to the blockchain and creating a contract account with a unique address. Once deployed, the bytecode stored at that address is immutable: it cannot be altered. This permanence offers strong guarantees about behavior but also makes bugs permanent at that address. The chapter warns that rigorous testing and auditing must happen before deployment; otherwise, a vulnerability or logic error can cause irreversible harm. In many cases, resolving a discovered bug requires deploying a new contract and migrating state or users to the new address. That migration can be complex and expensive, especially if funds are involved. As you prepare to deploy, double-check compiler versions, review the ABI and bytecode artifacts, and test interactions in a local or test network. Consider using design patterns that enable controlled upgrades or migration strategies, but note that such patterns themselves must be implemented and audited carefully. The key operational insight is this trade-off: immutability increases trust for users but places additional responsibility on developers to prevent mistakes before publishing code. screens.title: Common Vulnerabilities and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter highlights several common mistakes that can lead to critical failures in deployed contracts. Examples mentioned include integer overflows and underflows, reentrancy vulnerabilities, and incorrect access control — each of which can enable attackers to drain funds or corrupt state. While the chapter does not prescribe specific libraries, the main takeaway is to rigorously test logic, review access restrictions, and include clear ownership or permission checks where appropriate. Audits and code reviews with external experts help uncover subtle issues that unit tests alone might miss. When planning releases, treat deployment as a milestone that follows a checklist: automated tests, manual review, test network deployment, and an audit if significant value is at stake. Remember that immutability means vulnerabilities are permanent at that address, so prevention is far cheaper than remediation. A helpful mindset is to design minimal state and simple interfaces, reducing the attack surface. Before publishing, ask: who can call each function, what values may be passed, and what happens if a transaction fails mid-execution? fullNarratorScript:
Smart contracts are small programs that run on the blockchain and enforce rules without intermediaries. In practice that means once a contract is deployed it will execute exactly as coded, for anyone who calls it, on every node — a property that delivers trust but also requires discipline. In this lesson we focus on the Solidity basics you need to write, compile, and deploy simple contracts safely. You will learn the building blocks of a contract: the pragma compiler line, the contract block itself, state variables that persist on-chain, functions that change or read state, and events that let off-chain applications react without repeatedly polling state. You will also see the typical artifacts produced by compilation — the ABI and the bytecode — and why they matter to front‑end code like Web3. js. As we proceed, keep two ideas in mind: immutability means code can’t be changed after deployment, and deterministic execution means the same inputs produce the same outputs across all nodes. By the end you should be able to write a minimal contract, compile it in Remix, and explain the implications of publishing code on-chain. What would you do differently when every change is permanent?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to define what a smart contract is and explain its key characteristics, including immutability, transparency, and deterministic execution. You will understand why those properties matter for trust and what trade-offs they impose on development. You will also be able to identify common Solidity data types such as integers, addresses, booleans, strings, mappings, structs, and enums, and choose appropriate types for simple storage needs. Finally, you will write and interpret simple contract structures, including state variables, functions, and events, and understand how compilation produces the ABI and bytecode used by front-end libraries. Each objective includes a practical competency milestone so you can verify your work in Remix and reflect on design choices before deploying to any live network. Learning Objectives means knowledge and practice: define smart contracts, use solidity types, author basic contracts, and inspect compiled artifacts.. In practical terms, what you will be able to do after completing this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These objectives focus on practical verification and safe deployment thinking. You will practice writing and interpreting simple Solidity contracts so you can identify state variables, functions and events in a real file. You will compile code and inspect the ABI and bytecode artifacts, learning how the ABI maps to callable functions and events used by front‑end libraries. You will learn to recognize function visibility and function mutability keywords — public, private, internal, external, view, pure, and payable — and why they change who can call a function and whether it changes state or accepts Ether. Finally, you will learn to plan for immutability: testing, auditing, and the deployment workflow you need because you cannot modify a contract's code once it is published. Each card below links the skill to a concrete milestone you can verify in Remix to confirm competency.

A smart contract is a program that lives on a blockchain and executes automatically according to its code. It is self‑executing in the sense that the rules and outcomes are written into the code itself; once deployed, that code runs deterministically across every node. The chapter emphasizes three important guarantees: immutability, transparency, and deterministic execution. Immutability means the deployed code cannot be changed, so any logic you publish becomes permanent. Transparency means transactions and state changes are publicly verifiable on the blockchain, enabling anyone to audit behavior. Deterministic execution ensures the same inputs produce the same results across all nodes, which is how trustless agreement is achieved. A helpful analogy is a vending machine: drop in the right coin and the machine dispenses the selected item exactly as programmed. A common misconception is to confuse immutability of code with immutability of state; while the code cannot be changed, the contract’s state can be updated through function calls governed by its logic. Finally, consider why these guarantees matter: they remove intermediaries but place the burden of correctness on code quality, testing, and audit. Reflect: what checks would you add before making a contract public?

When you author Solidity you start with a pragma line that pins the compiler version, then write a contract block containing state, functions, and events. The compiler translates that human-readable Solidity into EVM bytecode and produces an ABI that describes the contract’s functions and events in a machine-readable JSON array. Deploying the compiled bytecode publishes it to the blockchain as a contract account with a unique address; that address is what your front-end libraries call. The ABI is essential for Web3. js because it tells the library how to encode function calls and decode event logs. In practice, use Remix or another compiler to generate the artifacts. Inspect the compilation details to copy the ABI and the bytecode. A common misconception is to confuse the ABI with bytecode — the ABI is an interface description, the bytecode is the executable that runs on the EVM. Finally, remember deployment permanence: once the bytecode is stored at an address, the code itself cannot be changed. If you discover a bug later, the remedy is to deploy a corrected contract and migrate state if needed. How would you design an upgrade path knowing code is immutable?

A Solidity source file is organized much like a small class-based program. It usually starts with a pragma declaration that sets the compiler version. Next comes the contract block — the primary container that holds state variables, functions, and events. State variables are stored on-chain; declaring a variable as public makes a simple getter available automatically. Functions encapsulate logic and can be marked with visibility and mutability keywords such as public, private, view, pure, or payable. Events are declared to emit log entries for off‑chain listeners. A helpful mental hierarchy is: file → contract → state + functions + events. For example, a state variable like uint public storedData is permanently stored on-chain and can be updated by a function like set. Events do not change state but provide an efficient mechanism for external applications to react to changes without repeatedly querying stored values. A common mistake is to mix up mutability keywords: marking a function view does not allow it to change state. When designing contracts, map the responsibilities of each element clearly so off‑chain code and users will interact with your contract safely and predictably.

Let's walk through a minimal contract to ground the structure in real code. The contract declares a public unsigned integer state variable, functions to set and get its value, an event declaration, and a function that updates the variable while emitting that event. The public state variable produces a getter automatically, so off‑chain code can read storage without writing a custom function. The setter function updates state and will cost gas when called on-chain. The update-and-emit function captures the old value, stores the new one, and emits an event that logs the change and the changer address. Events are efficient for notifying front‑end code because a dApp can subscribe to event logs rather than continuously reading state. A common misconception is assuming events themselves change contract state — they do not; they are logs. Finally, before deploying any contract with state-changing functions think about who should be allowed to call them and under what conditions. This walkthrough connects the code to the real operational and integration concerns you will face while building dApps. SimpleStorage: Read, Write, and Emit means a simple contract demonstrates state variables, setters/getters, and events used to notify off‑chain systems when state changes.. In practical terms, a line-by-line look at a minimal contract example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The chapter offers a hands-on activity using a greeting contract to practice writing, compiling, and inspecting artifacts. In this contract a string state variable greeting holds text on-chain, a setter updates it using a memory parameter for safe temporary storage, and a getter returns the stored greeting as a view function. The contract also declares an event that logs the old and new greetings and the address that performed the update. Solidity provides a set of primitive and composite types you will use to model on‑chain data. The chapter lists the commonly used ones: unsigned and signed integers (uint, int), address, bool, string, bytes, mapping, struct, and enum. Use uint for counters or balances, and address to represent account identifiers. Booleans represent binary states, and strings or bytes hold textual or raw data when necessary. Mapping is a built-in key-value storage mechanism useful for lookups, while struct lets you bundle related fields into a single composite type. Enum defines a set of named constant values for limited states. A common design consideration is gas cost: larger or complex types cost more to store and update, so avoid storing large strings unless required. Another misconception is assuming mappings are iterable — they are not; mappings are optimized for lookup but do not provide built-in enumeration. Choose types with both correctness and on‑chain cost in mind. Think about how your front-end will read and present stored values, and how events might be used to emit human-friendly logs instead of expensive on‑chain storage in some cases.

Understanding function visibility and mutability is crucial to controlling who can call your contract and what those calls may do. Visibility keywords determine who can invoke a function: public makes the function callable from everywhere, private restricts it to the contract that defines it, internal allows derived contracts to access it, and external optimizes for calls from other contracts or transactions. Mutability modifiers describe whether a function reads or changes state: view functions promise not to modify state and can be called off‑chain without a transaction; pure functions promise not to even read state and are purely computational. Payable marks a function as able to receive Ether; without it, any attempt to send Ether will revert. A frequent misconception is to assume public always implies safe — public simply means accessible; you still need access control logic to avoid unauthorized modifications. When designing functions, combine visibility and mutability appropriately: mark read-only helpers as view or pure to allow free, local calls, and mark functions that must accept funds as payable while carefully validating inputs and access rights. Events are a mechanism for contracts to record information that off‑chain applications can observe efficiently. When a contract emits an event, the data is stored in transaction logs that nodes keep; dApps and services listen for these logs rather than polling contract storage continuously. Events are especially useful for recording activity like state changes, transfers, or important actions where the front-end must react. In our examples the DataChanged or GreetingUpdated events log the previous value, the new value, and the address that made the change. Note that events do not change on‑chain storage — they are supplemental logs. A common misunderstanding is to use events as the primary source of truth for critical on‑chain data; events may be archived or indexed differently by clients, so store crucial data in contract state if the protocol requires on‑chain verification. Events are excellent for activity streams, UI updates, and efficient audit trails for off‑chain systems. When designing events, include indexed fields strategically so listeners can filter logs efficiently without scanning every block. Deploying a contract means publishing compiled bytecode to the blockchain and creating a contract account with a unique address. Once deployed, the bytecode stored at that address is immutable: it cannot be altered. This permanence offers strong guarantees about behavior but also makes bugs permanent at that address. The chapter warns that rigorous testing and auditing must happen before deployment; otherwise, a vulnerability or logic error can cause irreversible harm. In many cases, resolving a discovered bug requires deploying a new contract and migrating state or users to the new address. That migration can be complex and expensive, especially if funds are involved. As you prepare to deploy, double-check compiler versions, review the ABI and bytecode artifacts, and test interactions in a local or test network. Consider using design patterns that enable controlled upgrades or migration strategies, but note that such patterns themselves must be implemented and audited carefully. The key operational insight is this trade-off: immutability increases trust for users but places additional responsibility on developers to prevent mistakes before publishing code. The chapter highlights several common mistakes that can lead to critical failures in deployed contracts. Examples mentioned include integer overflows and underflows, reentrancy vulnerabilities, and incorrect access control — each of which can enable attackers to drain funds or corrupt state. While the chapter does not prescribe specific libraries, the main takeaway is to rigorously test logic, review access restrictions, and include clear ownership or permission checks where appropriate. Audits and code reviews with external experts help uncover subtle issues that unit tests alone might miss. When planning releases, treat deployment as a milestone that follows a checklist: automated tests, manual review, test network deployment, and an audit if significant value is at stake. Remember that immutability means vulnerabilities are permanent at that address, so prevention is far cheaper than remediation. A helpful mindset is to design minimal state and simple interfaces, reducing the attack surface. Let's recap three central ideas from this chapter. First: a smart contract is a self-executing program stored on the blockchain that enforces rules without intermediaries, relying on code correctness and deterministic execution. Second: immutability means once the contract bytecode is published at an address it cannot be altered, which strengthens trust but requires rigorous testing because bugs may be permanent. Third: deterministic execution ensures identical results across nodes for the same inputs, enabling predictable, trustless behavior. These ideas form the conceptual foundation for why smart contracts shift trust from third parties to code and why development practices like testing, code review, and careful type selection are so important. Carry these concepts forward when you design contract interfaces and plan deployment strategies.
